speaker: Derek Lowe
title: Derek Lowe, PhD: A Medicinal Chemist’s Thoughts on Drug Discovery and the Future of Pharma
question: In big pharma, why do public financial charts often show companies spending more on marketing than on R&D?
guest: One thing to remember is that the marketing budgets you see often include a lot of other expenses dumped into them, because that's usually SG&A—selling, general, and administrative all together. Companies do not have to break that down more specifically into what was actually spent on marketing and selling, so they don't, which makes those figures larger than they are in real life. At the same time, if you look at the percent of sales or profits spent on R&D compared to other industries, the drug industry spends a lot on marketing, but it also spends a hell of a lot on R&D. Companies we think of as great technological innovators like Apple spend nowhere near the percentage of their revenues on R&D that a typical large drug company does—factors of three, four, and five-fold lower. And the selling expense is partly high because of patent lifetimes. Every one of our small-molecule drugs is under a ticking clock with limited market exclusivity, and then it goes generic—even Lipitor, the single biggest selling drug in the world, went generic. So we spend heavily in both directions because the industry has to.

points.core: Reported marketing figures actually reflect broader SG&A accounting categories containing non-marketing overhead.
points.note: Accept: SG&A bundling administrative and general costs into what critics label marketing, since firms need not disaggregate pure ad spend. Do not credit: generic claims that financial reports are misleading without mentioning SG&A bundling.

points.core: Pharmaceutical companies invest a vastly higher revenue share in R&D than tech giants.
points.note: Accept: pharma R&D-to-revenue ratios being roughly 3x to 5x higher than major tech firms like Apple, showing high spend in both areas. Do not credit: vague statements that R&D is expensive without cross-industry revenue-share comparison.

points.core: Finite drug patent cliffs force heavy commercial spending to maximize short exclusivity windows.
points.note: Accept: ticking patent clocks and sudden generic revenue collapse compelling rapid commercial adoption before exclusivity expires. Do not credit: generic claims about corporate greed or consumer advertising.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because of how the numbers are categorized. Those charts typically compare R&D against "selling, general and administrative" (SG&A) expense, the line item companies report in their financial statements. SG&A is not just marketing: it bundles advertising and sales-force costs with executive pay, legal, finance, IT, HR, distribution, and other corporate overhead. Since companies rarely break out pure marketing, chart-makers use SG&A as a proxy, which overstates marketing spend considerably.

That said, the comparison isn't purely an artifact. Promotion in pharma is genuinely expensive: large sales forces visiting physicians, free samples, medical conferences, and, in the US, direct-to-consumer advertising. A patented drug has a limited exclusivity window, so companies spend heavily to maximize sales before generics arrive, and the marginal return on promoting an approved drug is often more certain than on risky early research.

Two further factors skew the picture: big pharma increasingly acquires drugs from biotechs, and those purchase costs mostly don't appear as R&D expense, while R&D itself runs around 15–25% of revenue, high relative to most industries.

points.why: The response explains that charts overstate marketing spending by using SG&A, which includes corporate overhead.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Public financial charts typically pull numbers straight from corporate income statements, creating a distorted comparison for two main accounting reasons alongside commercial realities. First, drugmakers rarely report "marketing" as a standalone line item; instead, charts relabel "Selling, General, and Administrative" (SG&A) expenses as marketing. While SG&A includes consumer ads, sales reps, and free drug samples, it also bundles massive non-marketing overhead—executive and administrative pay, legal and patent defense, regulatory compliance, IT, finance, and global facilities. True promotional spending is only a fraction of SG&A.

Second, big pharma increasingly outsources early discovery by acquiring smaller biotechs rather than developing every drug in-house. Under standard accounting rules, billions spent buying companies with late-stage or approved drugs are capitalized on the balance sheet as intangible assets and goodwill rather than expensed on the income statement’s R&D line. Lumping all corporate overhead into "marketing" inflates apparent promotional spend while acquisition accounting hides externalized research—even though drugmakers still genuinely spend heavily on physician sales forces to maximize revenue before patents expire.

noweb.answer: Public financial charts showing big pharma spending more on marketing than on R&D largely stem from how corporate accounting groups expenses. On standard income statements, pharmaceutical companies rarely report marketing as a standalone figure; instead, they bundle advertising and sales forces into Selling, General, and Administrative (SG&A) expenses. Many viral charts relabel that entire SG&A line as "marketing," even though it also covers massive non-promotional overhead like legal costs, human resources, IT, accounting, facilities, regulatory compliance, and executive pay. Meanwhile, the R&D line item often understates total spending on external innovation. Big pharma acquires a substantial share of its pipeline by buying smaller biotech firms or licensing promising compounds, and under accounting rules, multibillion-dollar acquisitions are generally capitalized on the balance sheet rather than recorded as routine R&D operating expenses. While drugmakers undeniably spend billions pitching to doctors and running consumer ads, the appearance that marketing eclipses research mostly comes from comparing all corporate overhead against internal R&D alone.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Partly it's how the charts are labeled, and partly companies really do spend that much on selling.

**The labeling problem.** Most viral charts compare R&D to "SG&A" (selling, general and administrative expenses) and call the whole SG&A line "marketing." But SG&A also covers executive pay, legal and regulatory costs, IT, distribution, and other overhead. Pure promotion is only part of it. R&D can also look smaller than it really is, because drugs bought through acquisitions or licensing deals are often booked as acquisition costs or intangible assets, not R&D.

**The real spending.** Selling costs are still huge. A patent gives a company a limited window of exclusive sales, so it's pushed to grab revenue quickly before generics arrive. Many drugs compete with similar products in the same class, so sales reps visiting doctors, conferences, free samples (often valued at retail price) and US direct-to-consumer TV ads are seen as necessary to win market share. Marketing also brings a quick, measurable return, while R&D is slow and usually fails.

The picture is changing. Several big companies, such as Merck, Roche and AstraZeneca, now report R&D spending close to or above their selling costs.
